title: Can Higher Education Be Sustainable if Academic Lives Are Not? Care, Online Teaching and Non-Linear Academic Careers
content: This conceptual article argues that higher education sustainability depends on sustainable academic lives. Drawing on feminist perspectives on care, academic labour and temporal justice, it examines how uninterrupted productivity, geographical mobility and continuous availability shape dominant models of academic work. Motherhood and other caring responsibilities are treated not as additional personal circumstances but as an analytical lens on the limits of those models. Online teaching is conceptualised as a social infrastructure redistributing participation across place, and asynchronous teaching as a temporal and communicative infrastructure redistributing time, workload, responsibility and modes of pedagogical presence. Online teaching may widen participation by reducing dependence on geographical mobility, supporting re-entry after interruption and enabling distributed and international collaboration. Asynchronous teaching may offer temporal flexibility for academics with caring responsibilities, but it also transfers responsibility for organising time, availability and boundaries to academics. Its workload is temporally asymmetric: concentrated before teaching begins, dispersed across interactions during delivery and prolonged after teaching periods end. Three reflexive auto-socio-biographical vignettes provide situated entry points rather than self-contained empirical evidence. The article concludes that flexibility becomes sustainable only when institutions recognise invisible and distributed labour, protect temporal boundaries, support online pedagogy and legitimise non-linear academic careers.
